knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $2{x}^{2}$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of ${x}^{3}-7.$ But the derivative is $3{x}^{2},$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{3}-7.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{2}{3}\text{d}u=2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{3}-7}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{3}-7}\cdot 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{4}{9}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{({x}^{3}-7)^{3}}}{9}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Expression Involving a Power Function Multiplied by a Constant Multiple of Its Derivative

question.:question/worked-solution:
In this case, the $x$ that's outside the square root isn't quite the derivative of $({x}^{2}-16).$ But the derivative is $2x,$ so we're only out by a constant factor.

So we make the substitution

$$
u={x}^{2}-16.
$$

Its derivative is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =2x\,⟹\,\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u=x\,\text{d}x,\end{aligned}
$$

and we can now write our integral in terms of $u,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}\,\text{d}x & =\int \sqrt{{x}^{2}-16}\cdot x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can solve the integral in terms of $u$ and then write the final result in terms of $x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int {u}^{1/2}\,\text{d}u & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{3/2}}{(\frac{3}{2})}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{u}^{3/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{({x}^{2}-16)^{3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
